synopsis: AAA supplies independent on-road evidence and a practical measurement method: its 2024 protocols monitor brake-pedal force to confirm driver braking, while its nighttime tests exposed performance cliffs missed by standard daytime protocols [f6325, f7974]. In October 2019, none of four vehicles avoided a pedestrian target at night at 25 mph; a study published 16 October 2025 reported improvement from 0% to 60% nighttime impact avoidance, still leaving roughly 40% failures under ideal conditions [f7975, f7977]. The 2025 study tested four named vehicles at 25 mph (40 km/h), with the Toyota Camry avoiding impact in every nighttime run and the Chevrolet Malibu ranking lowest [f7976, f7978, f7979]. High-visibility clothing caused complete detection loss in some systems, and both clothing and nighttime conditions were under-represented in consumer protocols, illustrating why physical or virtual protocol-based evidence can give false confidence outside its tested envelope [f7980, f7981, f7982]. The skeptic's review separately records that AAA ADAS repair studies were not verified, leaving that evidence stream unresolved [f10812].
